column2: Correspondence preserved in the JAAF Archives.

Albers replies to Barr by telegram and defines his three terms: structure (the inherent character of the raw material: wood grain, the fiber of thread, the crystal of marble), facture (an appearance governed by the working of the material: hammered metal, twisted wire, combed hair), texture (similar elements combined into a constructive unit: weaving, braiding, knitting, masonry) Telegram; examples: wood grain, the fiber of thread, the crystal of marble, hammered metal, twisted wire, combed hair, weaving, braiding, knitting, masonry

The Brooklyn Daily Eagle publishes an article about an art professor fleeing the Nazis who has come to teach — press evidence of the Alberses' emigration. headline, in translation: art professor, fleeing the Nazis, here to teach
Albers's speech at a college fund-raising luncheon in New York.

Part of the faculty is trying to oust Rice and threatens to break up the college if he does not leave; the stated reason: he insults and alienates donors and students; the real reason, in her view: his disciples have felt betrayed since the previous year and are seeking security in success; personal rivalries on top of that; Rice was the college, which no longer holds people together; Allan Sly will not return next year, seeking security and reputation, which hits the college hard since music has been the most important thing of the year; she is expecting a new teacher, as Sly has become an inhibiting force for her: his unattainable standards paralyze her at the piano explosion expected within six weeks Consequences: Sly's departure announced, Rice's prestige declining, speculation about another school founded by his followers

A few months before the war, the Fleischmanns leave Nazi Germany on the same ship, the Orinoco, as two years earlier. Toni records in her diary the pain of final exile and moments of happiness regained (arrival in Mexico City, the tropical landscape). Toni's diary: “¿ahora qué?”; the ship Orinoco Consequences: The parents settle in Mexico

The Fleischmanns disembark from the Orinoco, the same ship they had taken on vacation two years earlier; Josef and Anni meet them at the port Words: Toni: two years ago today they had set out on the same voyage on the same ship; today they are leaving their native country, which they must leave forever Atmosphere: Twofold: the joy of reunion, the grief of exile Stakes: The wrenching emigration of the German family under Nazism

Anni's parents disembark from the Orinoco, the same ship as on their 1937 trip; Josef and Anni wait for them on the dock; Toni notes in her diary the contrast between the two voyages. Words: Toni: exactly two years ago, the same ship, the Orinoco; that was a trip to see their children again; today it is a departure from their homeland, which they must leave forever Atmosphere: Joy mixed with the despair of emigrants; the tropical countryside experienced as a magnificent, rare gift Stakes: The final exile of a German Jewish family
Albers's speech at the first general meeting at the start of the college's seventh year
Albers's opening speech at the start of the college's 7th year.
Scott, an instructor at Harvard, writes enthusiastically to Albers after a design workshop.
Albers delivers the speech “On Education and Art Education”; typescript preserved in the archives of the Josef and Anni Albers Foundation. Typescript, JAAF Archive
Albers reads an untitled text at the Black Mountain College meeting held at the Museum of Modern Art. Text preserved in the JAAF Archives.
Albers's address at a Black Mountain College meeting held at the Museum of Modern Art. Text preserved at the Albers Foundation, 3 pages.

Fund-raising meeting: Gropius describes his stay at Black Mountain and the spirit of cooperation in meetings with the students; with Breuer he presents the model of the glass houses on stilts; Albers, as star visitor, sets out his educational creed; Herald Tribune photographers snap the two architects around the model. Words: Gropius: “letting the life form the house”; Albers: “One can suffocate from knowledge, never from experience” Atmosphere: New York elegance, descriptive idealism, a model in the spotlight Stakes: The mountain college sold to America

New York Herald Tribune article showing Breuer and Gropius with the model of a new building planned for the Lake Eden campus. article of January 10, 1940, with the model Consequences: the building is not built as planned; the Studies Building will be built around 1940-41

“Tradition and Technique Are Watchwords at Yale's School of the Fine Arts”: an opening photo shows advanced sculpture students drawing a nude model; realistic paintings of the nude; students learning framing and gilding; one grinds his colors with a mortar; a fourth-year student dresses a mannequin to study the effect of drapery over its knees. Life, February 12, 1940, pp. 44-47.

At the Valentine's Day party, the students' costumes strikingly resemble the material studies done in class earlier that day; Albers documents them in color slides. Community life and teaching merge, as at the Bauhaus.

In February 1940, Rice having extended his leave without resigning, Wunsch writes the letter that ends the struggle: his resignation would be appreciated; Rice had promised to send it if it was needed to keep the college from closing; half the faculty refuses to face another internal struggle on top of economic insecurity; it all comes down to a loss of confidence in his ability to work in a small community. To Nell, separately: Rice is responsible for this loss of confidence; God knows they did not want to lose it; without him, they will feel less downcast and more independent. Letters of February 16, 1940. Consequences: Rice's resignation.

Wunsch writes to Rice asking for the promised resignation, citing half of an exhausted faculty and the loss of confidence; to Nell, a separate letter explains that Rice alone is responsible. Words: it all comes down to this: they have lost confidence in his ability to work in a small community like this one; to Nell: God knows they did not want to lose confidence in him. Atmosphere: sad firmness Stakes: The founder's final expulsion
Albers declares that at Black Mountain the teaching of art is at the center of all activity, a point of internal dispute Consequences: At stake in the future schism of art versus letters and sciences
John Dewey writes a letter to Theodore Dreier, quoted in the main text

A five-day workshop titled “Fundamental Design of Today,” transcribed; Albers repeats in it the Rembrandt anecdote already published in 1934; he had also dealt with drawing in an unpublished text, “Drawing,” the same year. Complete transcript preserved (JA Papers). Consequences: His BMC teaching spreads beyond the college.
Albers presents an untitled text at the college's first general meeting. Manuscript preserved, BMCR.
Untitled speech given at the college's first general meeting; typescript preserved.

Marcia Winn writes “Hardware Art Nicks Edge of Priority Knife”: amid wartime restrictions, the metal materials of Anni Albers's weaving compete with military priorities. Chicago Daily Tribune, November 15, 1941

Newspaper headline of April 4, 1942: “CLARENCE DAWSON BURIED HERE MON. Husband of Cara Byars Dawson Succumbs After Long Illness”; at the coffin, the child stares dry-eyed at his father's face — waxy skull, scarred, ugly — then turns his head away: “That's not my father”; a cool, rainy day; as the procession crosses town toward the cemetery, he watches through the window the April trees, the lawns, the houses, the cars; the air is cool and damp like the earth into which the coffin is lowered; at home, in the Victorian parlor with the curtains drawn, his mother sits in an upholstered armchair drinking a glass of sherry; the aunts stare at the floor; one of them is the first to tell him he will have to be a good boy. Sherry, upholstered armchair, drawn curtains

The child stares at the dead man's waxy face and turns his head away; a cool, rainy day; a procession through town, April trees seen through the window; in the Victorian parlor with the curtains drawn, the mother drinks a sherry, the aunts stare at the floor; an aunt tells him he will have to be a good boy. Words: “That's not my father”; he will have to be a good boy Atmosphere: Cool, damp air, Victorian silence, sherry Stakes: Repressed grief, dry eyes

The college writes to the National Selective Service Board to spare at least its older teachers from the draft; Major T. Upton replies on May 14 that each case will be decided individually by the local boards.
Fortune sends an inquiry by telegram; BMC replies on an undated typed page — a good profile of the war's effects on the college.
A telegram dated December 16, 1942, is decided on at the Board of Fellows meeting of the same day.
In a lecture, Albers discusses the artificiality of the single-viewpoint perspective built into camera lenses and describes photographs as the flattest kind of image
Dreier thanks Forbes for a gift of three thousand dollars and for his past help. $3,000
A conference planned at BMC is finally moved to Talladega College for reasons Duberman was unable to establish.
Dreier corresponds with Marshall Field (March 24, 1942, July 24, 1943), who offers 10,000 dollars; other appeals to the Babbotts and to John Burchard. Amount: $10,000

Invited by Albers in 1943, Charlot writes in his diary: on September 6, arrival at the Alberses', “fotos admirables de México”; on the 7th, his lecture on Mexico, a reception at the Alberses' with wine; he is asked to teach the following summer. Albers also organizes an exhibition of Charlot at BMC the same year. Charlot's diary, 1943; wine served at the reception Consequences: Charlot returns with his family the following summer

Invited by Albers, Charlot visits the college: on September 6 at the Alberses' (photos of Mexico admired); on the evening of the 7th, a lecture on Mexico, a reception at the Alberses' with wine; he is offered a teaching post for the following summer. Charlot's diary: “Sept. 6. To Albers... Evening: My talk on Mexico. The reception at Albers. Wine. I am asked to teach next summer.” Consequences: An exhibition of Charlot's work at the college later in the year; return the following summer

On the 6th, Charlot arrives at the Alberses' and admires his photographs of Mexico; on the evening of the 7th, he gives his lecture on Mexico, followed by a reception at the Alberses' with wine; he is offered a teaching post for the following summer Words: Charlot's diary: “Fotos admirables de México tomadas por él,” “Mi charla sobre México. La recepción en Albers. Vino. Me piden que dé clases el verano que viene” Atmosphere: Warm and convivial, over wine Stakes: Sealing Charlot's invitation to teach at BMC

On the 6th, Charlot goes to the Alberses' and admires his photos of Mexico; on the evening of the 7th, he gives his lecture on Mexico, followed by a reception at the Alberses' with wine; he is offered a teaching post for the following summer. Words: Charlot's diary: “Evening: My talk on Mexico. The reception at Albers. Wine. I am asked to teach next summer.” Atmosphere: Convivial and warm, over wine and images of Mexico Stakes: Mexico enters the college in the person of Charlot; the beginning of a friendship and a collaboration (the 1944 frescoes)

A wedding two years and two days after Pearl Harbor. Witnesses: her brother Peter, her father, Bart Vanderschellen (a Dutchman who had fought in the Spanish Civil War), and Alain, the New Yorker cartoonist (Daniel Brustlein). Then a drink in a downtown bar, without ceremony, and back to the studio, where each returns to work. Marie Fried, the mother, refuses to attend. Elaine tells Gruen she was twenty-three; she was twenty-five Consequences: a union whose tensions everyone foresees

A December morning: a navy-blue dress already worn, her sister's handbag, a $9.50 wedding ring, no mother and no Conrad; then either a bar or a cafeteria lunch paid for by Biala and Brustlein; straight back to work at the studio Words: Elaine will note that the day is Emily Dickinson's birthday and falls two years and two days after Pearl Harbor Atmosphere: perfunctory, without ceremony, almost a festive non-event Stakes: the union of two painters who go back to work that same afternoon

The rector walks into the lobby where the students are celebrating New Year's; too much wine has, in his view, turned the “little boys and girls” into embracing Greenwich Villagers; he leaves at once, deeply upset, and tells John Evarts about it Words: Wunsch: “too much wine had changed the little boys and girls into Greenwich Villagers”; “I didn't stay very long” Atmosphere: A student party seen through a stern, prudish eye Stakes: The conflict between order and sensuality at the heart of the community in wartime
First reading in English of the play (not named here), given at the college.

Gropius writes to Dreier; the letter, preserved in the Bauhaus Archive in Berlin, is evidence of their steady correspondence during the war. Letter of April 16, 1944, Bauhaus Archive, Berlin Consequences: Keeps up the relationship that will lead Dreier to include Gropius in the mailing of his resignation

At a faculty meeting, Straus declares that there are definite things to be faced about Black people: they are strange, and the formula that we are all human beings is too small and too simple; he does not mean that we are superior, but that there are definite differences; he doubts that it is the college's role to change these things. Typed notes of the meeting Consequences: Some call him a racist (anonymously)

Albers writes to René d'Harnoncourt (MoMA): to eliminate friction and percussion, it would be good, even necessary, to admit students of the red and yellow races as well — Indians, Chinese, Japanese Americans; that way the move would not look like opposition to racial prejudice and would lose its character of aggression. Consequences: Reveals the fear of going too far too fast

In a letter to John Evarts of July 8, 1944, Wunsch describes the first day of Kolisch's workshop as a “privilege”: disagreements over the interpretation of a phrase, discussions, explanations, hard and concentrated work; for him, a dramatic adventure to watch order emerge from work.

A series of regular and special faculty meetings at the height of the crisis; the Lowinskys remember sharing Anni Albers's indignation at Frances de Graaff's irresponsibility. Minutes in the Raleigh Archives; interview with the Lowinskys of April 10, 1967. Consequences: Escalation toward the sanctions and departures of August 1944.
A note dated July 19, 1944, is deposited in the Raleigh Archives; Gregory remembers it (interview of June 18, 1967).

According to an account that may not be quoted, the Board had reckoned that Frances would not leave if Bentley left, but that Bentley would leave if Frances left — hence the fire directed at her. According to two anonymous witnesses, Anni Albers counted votes behind the scenes (the one who counted noses and figured it would work was Anni, one says) and had the compromises replayed; she never spoke much in public. Special Board meetings of August 1, 6, and 8, 1944. Consequences: The departures of Bentley and de Graaff.

Jalowetz writes to the Board of Fellows on August 14, 1944; Wunsch confirms that his sympathies lay with those leaving. Bentley describes him as someone who could not live with hostility. Also a four-page typed statement by Jalowetz, undated.
Martin comes straight from the station just as Bodky is playing the first twelve fugues of the second book of the Well-Tempered Clavier. He walks from the station to the place of the performance

A five-page document summarizing the discussions of the work program at the community meeting of Tuesday, November 13, 1945. Consequences: Followed by the “Recommendations of Community Meeting” of November 27, 1945; launch of a faculty study group on the aims of education at BMC, whose planned second meeting never took place

Wallen describes his scheme (“three-step process”) in a letter to his parents: first identify the symptoms, then examine the underlying causes, and finally write prescriptions to treat the problem. Letter of March 25, 1946; also a one-page notice handed out before the meeting

Gropius writes to Albers to thank him for guiding his daughter, helping her to combine her talent for abstract thought with her visual talent. Letter preserved in the Western Regional Archives, Asheville.

Article “It's Art, Baby” by Robert C. Rouark in the Philadelphia Evening Bulletin (September 27, 1946); preceded in May 1946 by an article, “Black Mountain College,” in Junior Bazaar (pp. 130-133 ff.). Consequences: The college gains coverage in the mainstream press
The last letter to Perdekamp quoted; interviews with the BBC (June 21, 1968), Finkelstein (January 2 and November 2, 1966), and Duberman (November 11, 1967) serving as sources for the book.
Sawyer's appointment is confirmed in the minutes of the Yale Council of April 19, 1947, under the presidency of Charles Seymour. Consequences: He recruits Albers in 1950
A three-page letter from Levi; Albers writes in pencil at the top of the first page: “Consider [this] partly an answer of the board [of fellows]”. Three pages; pencil annotation; JAAF archive

Albers receives Levi's three pages, takes a pencil, and writes at the top of the first page that this is partly an answer from the Board of Fellows Words: Annotation: “Consider [this] partly an answer of the board [of fellows]” Atmosphere: Administrative coldness Stakes: The Levi-Albers conflict enters the record

Albers writes to Ted and Bobbie Dreier; the Dreiers' replies are lost or destroyed. The college's financial situation is complicated. The Dreier family holds a second mortgage of 16,500 dollars on the Black Mountain property Consequences: Background to Albers's taking over the rectorship
In a letter to the Board of Fellows, Albers asks to be paid at least $1000 for his work in the second semester. $1000 minimum, second semester
Goodman signs in New York a series of ironic precepts addressed to anyone planning to create a Universe. dated and signed “New York City June 1, 1947”

In a confidential letter to Ise Gropius, Dreier raises the possibility of settling in postwar Germany, while still hoping that things will work out at Black Mountain. Letter of August 22, 1947, Bauhaus Archive, Berlin Consequences: Shows Dreier's discouragement a year before his resignation

A sled bought for Johnny just in case; a miraculously white world in the morning; runs down the road, the students who stayed on campus take turns running alongside Johnny on the way down and pulling him back up; the gentle slope of the garden. Sleds are scarce; a sled tied to a laundry basket with both children, an overturn into a ditch, a cut under Frances's eye, treated at the infirmary by a student nurse with a curly light-brown beard, which she strokes without crying.

As they are about to set off, Cage and Cunningham find under their car a heap of presents — paintings, drawings, and all sorts of things — a sign of appreciation and affection. Atmosphere: Quiet emotion, mutual gratitude. Stakes: Sealing the invitation to return for the summer of 1948.

The committee meets on April 24-25, 1948; four members report on architecture, four on painting and sculpture (Albers, Elliott, Kratina, Osborn). The report of the chairman, Leslie Cheek Jr., recommends a basic curriculum for all new students; Albers's voice is recognizable in it: no formula to copy, develop one's own procedures through direct experience, “think in situations, not by predigested theory”. An appendix includes “Collaborative Problems” worked on in teams on a visual problem of the industrial age.

A handwritten letter to the college faculty assessing Nakata's oral and written work for the graduation examination; signed, among others, “Regis”. Reproduced in facsimile. Letterhead “Black Mountain College,” dated June 7, 1948. Consequences: Nakata's graduation.

At the special faculty meeting of July 12, 1948, Goldowski voices her annoyance at having been unable to learn from various members of the faculty which ideas could be considered representative of the college's principles. Consequences: A sign of the ideological confusion of the crisis

Letter from M.C. to the Dreiers of July 25, 1948 (including a fuller draft given to Duberman); in it she sets out the policy disagreement of expansion versus poverty, later elaborated by Stephen Forbes in interview (April 1-2, 1967). a partly unpublished draft Consequences: A key document of the 1948 crisis

Richards asks the Dreiers frankly whether she is wrong: do they intend to make BMC a sleek jewel of modern design — which costs money — when she would prefer disorder, more teachers, and fewer students? Words: tell her if she is wrong; she would prefer a ramshackle campus, more teachers, fewer students, and less money. Atmosphere: friendly frankness, deep disagreement Stakes: the direction of the college at stake, a year before the split

Richards translates Satie's play (1913) for its first production in English; it is performed with Fuller and Elaine de Kooning and directed by two of Richards's students, Helen Livingston and Arthur Penn. Consequences: Penn will become a Hollywood director (The Miracle Worker, 1962; Bonnie and Clyde, 1967)

At the faculty meetings of August 27 and 28, 1948, Albers says he hopes to obtain outside financial help (a pledge of 2,000 dollars already received) and to plan another art institute for the following summer with “a large number of students.” pledge of $2,000 Consequences: Will materialize as the 1949 Summer Institute

Dreier sends his resignation from Black Mountain College and includes Gropius on the mailing list, a sign of their closeness — the correspondence in the Bauhaus Archive tells of Dreier's disillusionment and of his departure from the radical institution he had done so much to create. Consequences: The end of the college's most difficult postwar period; the departure of a founding pillar

Dreier writes to the Gropiuses that the die is cast: he cannot bring himself to undertake another reorganization of the college and announces that he wants to leave. He includes the Gropiuses in the mailing of his letter of resignation, evidence of their closeness. A few days of reflection before the letter of August 31, 1948 Consequences: The cofounder resigns, fifteen years after the opening

After a few days of reaching his conclusions, Dreier writes to the Gropiuses that the die is cast: he cannot undertake another reorganization, he wants to leave; he includes the Gropiuses in the official mailing of his resignation, then stays on for a time for the transition to Albers. Words: the die is finally cast; he has said that he wants to leave. Atmosphere: Quiet resolve after fifteen years of struggle Stakes: The cofounder leaves his life's work
An untitled handwritten manuscript bearing the note “September 11, 1948 BMC” Handwritten document preserved at the Albers Foundation
Albers's handwritten manuscript dated September 11, 1948: education, like art, means order, as opposed to chaos, dirt, and confusion.

Lanier writes to Asawa to justify his refusal to become a partner in the Tin Angel: such a venture would harm his standing as an architect. Quotation: “What would have happened to Bill de Kooning if he had taken a job as a jewelry salesman” Consequences: He turns down Tolk-Watkins's offer of a partnership

Six outsiders invited to discuss their role as trustees: day 1 in questions (the cause of student turnover, legal responsibilities in North Carolina, guarantees that the internal troubles will stop); day 2 in suggestions: tuition raised to $1,800, loan funds instead of reductions, maximum aid capped at $900, a loan against the property, strong fields in art, music, and writing with a visiting faculty, a campaign of quick and dramatic publicity, an alumni organization, a concrete program and budget. They ask for another month before committing themselves. tuition $1,800; aid capped at $900. Consequences: The decision is postponed to January 1949.

Day one: questions about student turnover, legal responsibilities in North Carolina, guarantees against further internal troubles; day two: budget and program suggestions, then a refusal to commit before checking. Words: can assurances be given that internal troubles will not keep arising at Black Mountain? Atmosphere: Cautious mistrust, an audit Stakes: The college must submit to the outside scrutiny it has always shunned
Letter preserved in the archives of Ruth Asawa Lanier, Inc., cited by the source. Document dated January 6, 1949

The “Annual Report Blank of North Carolina Colleges” form of January 13, 1949, in the Raleigh archives gives the enrollment figures; a new student (Kelly) found Albers very bitter about the departures: so many students leaving upset him more than the faculty departures. Consequences: Albers ready to take charge of the reorganization again

Pittenger, retired treasurer of Swarthmore, friend and confidant of Frank Aydelotte (Nell Rice's brother, a longtime adviser to the founders), sent by Aydelotte to look into the school's options; he stays from January 27 to 30 but does not attend the meeting of the 29th. A 4-day stay Consequences: A harsh report on the faculty
The letter announcing the meeting had been sent to them in New York, care of Albers's dealer, Sidney Janis, but had not arrived in time. Consequences: A feeling of being kept out

The Alberses return from New York on January 27 and discover that a meeting on the fate of the college was held without them on January 14; the letter of invitation, sent to their dealer Sidney Janis, never arrived in time Atmosphere: A feeling of conspiracy and exclusion Stakes: Albers's power collapses; his departure in May is announced

Asawa opens the envelope: an aerial brochure of Sausalito, “city of homes,” with the location of the Tin Angel marked in Peggy's hand and a sarcastic “ha !” Words: Peggy's irony aimed at the word “homes” Atmosphere: Mocking distance from the dream of mass homeownership Stakes: Asawa, still at BMC, confronted with postwar domesticity

Pittenger writes to Aydelotte with barely veiled prejudice against Germans and against the elevation of art in the college; he calls Anni a “witch” and writes that Albers on his own is radically different from Albers with his wife; in a postscript: if Dreier leaves now, Albers will leave at the end of the semester. Consequences: Albers replies the same day (letter to Pittenger, February 1, 1949), then to the Committee of Friends on February 3
De Kooning reads a text titled “A Desperate View” at a Friday evening discussion of the new art school Subjects of the Artist. Text reproduced by Thomas B. Hess, p. 15.
A letter signed “Kim” addressed to “Leslie,” with the typed note “Copy for Mr. Albers” at the top of the sheet. Carbon copy, JAAF archives

According to Fuller, a second geodesic structure, fourteen feet (about 4.3 m) in diameter, erected in the garden of the Pentagon building. fourteen feet in diameter; reported in a letter to Dean Wells Bennett, University of Michigan, May 14, 1949
Lanier writes to his parents that nowhere is competition among architects as fierce as in California, and that the best work is demanded there.

Letter from Albert Lanier to Ruth Asawa dated April 20, 1949, preserved at Ruth Asawa Lanier, Inc. — from the period of their relationship, born around Black Mountain College. Letter of April 20, 1949

Breton denounces the United States' treatment of Black people and Indians, sexual hypocrisy, the Digests, Coca-Cola, the grip on Latin America, and the imperialist design on Europe. Coca-Cola and the Digests named explicitly
The new Board of Fellows sends an official letter to the Friends of the College announcing the new state of affairs. Consequences: The new leadership is institutionalized

Dreier tells Duberman (1967) that he was accused of trying to hand Black Mountain over to the University of North Carolina, simply because he had asked its president, Frank Graham, whether he would be interested in the college in the event of bankruptcy. Consequences: Feeds the distrust of Dreier

A three-page note by Fuller dated June 1, 1949, contains his remark about plumbing; the sale of gravel and the Forbes affair are documented in the Pittenger-Trayer correspondence (March 25 and 30, 1949). a 3-page note Consequences: Windfall income for the college

Sawyer's proposal discussed at a meeting on Saturday, July 9, 1949; Kahn develops “Collaborative Problem—1949: An Idea Center for Plastics” (manuscript dated “8.11”), annotated by Kahn. Bayer and Kauffer had been suggested as early as 1948. Typescript annotated by Kahn, Kahn Collection, University of Pennsylvania; letter from Albers to Sawyer of July 23, 1949 Consequences: Albers takes part; photos of Kahn with the students published in PAS, the 1950 yearbook of the architecture department

A letter (postmarked July 12, 1949) thanking them for the good time, reporting the visit of Mr. Kean with Dr. Penniman, who came the day before while he was working on a fresco, then complaining: the girls swear terribly, drink gin, call the boys dirty names; he was called “grandma” and pious; even the teachers use obscene language in class; a certain Arnold, though, is wonderful. A fresco in progress; gin; the nickname “grandma”; misspellings preserved

A letter (postmarked July 12, 1949) to his sister Ca and his brother-in-law Bill, printed with its original mistakes: Dawson is indignant that the girls drink gin and curse the boys, that he was called “grandma” and prim, that even the teachers swear, and that a brilliant man uses obscenity in a class. gin, beer tolerated, the nickname “grandma,” postmark July 12, 1949
